newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli crackdown on Palestinians over bombing.
newsitem.headline: Israeli crackdown on Palestinians over bombing.

text.p: Israel suspended peace talks over a Jerusalem suicide attack, made arrests and threatened to re-enter Palestinian areas to seize "terrorists" on Thursday if President Yasser Arafat's forces failed to do the job.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet demanded Arafat clamp down on Moslem militants responsible for double suicide bombings that killed 13 people and wounded 170 at a Jewish market on Wednesday.

"You can't move ahead in the political process while the Palestinian Authority is not taking the minimal action it promised against terrorist centres," Netanyahu said on Israel's Channel One television.
Israeli and Palestinian security forces arrested alleged Moslem militants in separate raids in the West Bank.

The Israeli army said its forces had detained 28 Palestinians overnight in connection with "hostile terrorist activities". It gave no details of the raids in Palestinian villages still under Israeli occupation.

Palestinian security officials said they had arrested at least 10 activists of the militant Islamic Jihad and Hamas movements in the PLO-ruled Bethlehem area. They said they made arrests in other areas under their control but gave no details.
Officials said Israeli-PLO security meetings took place late on Wednesday in the West Bank but they did not elaborate.
A leaflet issued in Hamas's name claimed responsibility for Wednesday's attack. Israeli pathologists were trying to identify the bodies of the two bombers.

In Jerusalem, mourners streamed to cemeteries for the funerals of victims of the deadliest attack on Israelis in over a year. Memorial candles flickered on a makeshift shrine at the spot where one of the bombs went off and walls were plastered with black-bordered funeral notices.
"The terrorism is back" read one front-page headline.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said U.S. President Bill Clinton's top Middle East advisers planned to meet later on Thursday to assess the status of the peace process but they were unlikely to present any recommendations.

In the West Bank town of Ramallah, the 88-member Palestinian Legislative Council added to pressures on Arafat by giving him one month to dissolve his cabinet and appoint a new one following a corruption probe.
Countries that have pledged millions of dollars in aid to Arafat's administration have set clean government as a condition for delivering the funds.

At Dahariyeh village near the West Bank city of Hebron, Israeli forces detained members of two Palestinian families whose two sons, both Islamic militants, have been missing for 15 months, relatives said. It was not immediately clear if the missing pair were the two suicide bombers.
Relatives of the two were taken by Israeli police to the forensic institute near Tel Aviv for tests to determine the bombers' identities, witnesses said.
Late on Wednesday, Netanyahu's security cabinet ordered a halt to peace moves and vowed to act.

"The cabinet decision is quite clear. If Israel has to, that is if the Palestinian Authority is not going to do what it is supposed to do against the terrorists, Israel will have to do it," Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan told Reuters.
"Israel will have to go into the areas controlled by the Palestinian Authority if that is necessary and get the terrorists there," he said.

Israel sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip immediately after the Jerusalem attack. Military checkpoints blocked movements of residents and tourists alike. Israel prevented Palestinian newspapers from being delivered to self-ruled Gaza.

A Palestinian security official said Arafat, who condemned the bombing, had declared a state of emergency in Palestinian areas and ordered the arrest of activists of "extremist groups" including Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

PLO officials said Israel's confiscation of lands and expansion of Jewish settlements had caused Palestinians despair and frustration. Peace talks have been stuck since March, when Netanyahu broke ground on a settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah insisted the Palestinian Authority was preventing attacks from being launched from areas under its control and warned Israel against "overstepping the red line" by entering Palestinian-controlled territory.
World leaders urged Israel and the Palestinians to press on with talks but U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross postponed a planned mission to salvage peacemaking during a period of national mourning.
Among Jewish shoppers in the market, the mood was a mixture of resignation and defiance. Miriam Goldberg said Arab bombs would not drive her away.
"These barbarians, animals of prey, want to throw us out of the country. We won't go," she said as soldiers and police patrolled nearby.
But she lamented: "How much longer? How much longer?"
